\subsection*{Randomized --- Matching Math: Results}

\begin{definition}[Bipartite graph of a Boolean matrix]
\lean{Randomized.Matching.bipartiteGraph}
\statementsource{Vad12}{pdf-bf2ce5422088-p018-b003}
\statementsource{arora-barak-ch07-randomized-computation}{pdf-26d95080dbde-p005-b005}
\label{Randomized.Matching.bipartiteGraph}
\leanok
For a natural number $n$ and an $n\times n$ Boolean matrix $A$, define a graph with
vertex set the disjoint union of two copies of $\{0,\ldots,n-1\}$. A vertex in the first
copy indexed by $i$ is adjacent to a vertex in the second copy indexed by $j$ exactly
when $A_{ij}$ is true; there are no other adjacent pairs.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[Adjacency across the bipartition]
\lean{Randomized.Matching.bipartiteGraph_adj_inl_inr}
\label{Randomized.Matching.bipartiteGraph_adj_inl_inr}
\leanok
\uses{Randomized.Matching.bipartiteGraph}
\difficulty{1}
For every natural number $n$, every Boolean matrix $A$ indexed by $	ext{Fin}(n) \times
\text{Fin}(n)$, and all $i,j \in \text{Fin}(n)$, the left vertex indexed by $i$ is
adjacent to the right vertex indexed by $j$ in the associated bipartite graph if and
only if $A_{ij}=\text{true}$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Adjacency across the bipartition]
\lean{Randomized.Matching.bipartiteGraph_adj_inr_inl}
\label{Randomized.Matching.bipartiteGraph_adj_inr_inl}
\leanok
\uses{Randomized.Matching.bipartiteGraph}
\difficulty{1}
For every natural number $n$, every Boolean matrix $A$ indexed by $\text{Fin}(n) \times
\text{Fin}(n)$, and all $i,j \in \text{Fin}(n)$, the right vertex indexed by $j$ is
adjacent to the left vertex indexed by $i$ in the associated bipartite graph if and only
if $A_{ij}=\text{true}$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[No Edges Within the Left Part]
\lean{Randomized.Matching.not_bipartiteGraph_adj_inl_inl}
\label{Randomized.Matching.not_bipartiteGraph_adj_inl_inl}
\leanok
\uses{Randomized.Matching.bipartiteGraph}
\difficulty{1}
Let $n$ be a natural number, let $A$ be a Boolean matrix indexed by
$	ext{Fin}(n)\times\text{Fin}(n)$, and let $i,j\in\text{Fin}(n)$. In the bipartite graph
specified by $A$, the left-part vertices indexed by $i$ and $j$ are not adjacent.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[No Edges Within the Right Part]
\lean{Randomized.Matching.not_bipartiteGraph_adj_inr_inr}
\label{Randomized.Matching.not_bipartiteGraph_adj_inr_inr}
\leanok
\uses{Randomized.Matching.bipartiteGraph}
\difficulty{1}
Let $n$ be a natural number, let $A$ be a Boolean matrix indexed by
$\text{Fin}(n)\times\text{Fin}(n)$, and let $i,j\in\text{Fin}(n)$. In the bipartite
graph specified by $A$, the right-part vertices indexed by $i$ and $j$ are not adjacent.
\end{theorem}

\begin{definition}[Perfect matching in a bipartite graph]
\lean{Randomized.Matching.HasPerfectMatching}
\statementsource{Vad12}{pdf-bf2ce5422088-p018-b003}
\statementsource{arora-barak-ch07-randomized-computation}{pdf-26d95080dbde-p005-b005}
\label{Randomized.Matching.HasPerfectMatching}
\leanok
\uses{Randomized.Matching.bipartiteGraph}
Let $n$ be a natural number and let $A$ be an $n\times n$ matrix with entries in
$\{\mathrm{false},\mathrm{true}\}$. The bipartite graph specified by $A$ has a perfect
matching if and only if it contains a subgraph that is a perfect matching.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[Perfect matchings and permutations]
\lean{Randomized.Matching.hasPerfectMatching_iff_exists_perm}
\label{Randomized.Matching.hasPerfectMatching_iff_exists_perm}
\leanok
\uses{Randomized.Matching.HasPerfectMatching, Randomized.Matching.bipartiteGraph, Randomized.Matching.not_bipartiteGraph_adj_inl_inl, Randomized.Matching.not_bipartiteGraph_adj_inr_inr}
\difficulty{6}
Let $n$ be a natural number and let $A$ be an $n\times n$ Boolean matrix. The bipartite
graph with an edge from left vertex $i$ to right vertex $j$ exactly when $A_{ij}$ is
true has a perfect matching if and only if there is a permutation $\sigma$ of the
indices such that $A_{i,\sigma(i)}$ is true for every $i$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{definition}[Edmonds matrix]
\lean{Randomized.Matching.edmondsMatrix}
\statementsource{Vad12}{pdf-bf2ce5422088-p019-b001}
\statementsource{arora-barak-ch07-randomized-computation}{pdf-26d95080dbde-p006-b001}
\label{Randomized.Matching.edmondsMatrix}
\leanok
Let $n$ be a natural number, let $R$ be a commutative semiring, and let $A$ be an
$n\times n$ Boolean matrix. The associated polynomial matrix has entry $X_{ij}$ when
$A_{ij}$ is true and $0$ otherwise, where the variables $X_{ij}$ are indexed by pairs in
$\{0,\ldots,n-1\}^2$ and the entries are polynomials over $R$.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Monomial of a permutation matching]
\lean{Randomized.Matching.matchMono}
\statementsource{arora-barak-ch07-randomized-computation}{pdf-26d95080dbde-p006-b001}
\label{Randomized.Matching.matchMono}
\leanok
Let $n$ be a natural number and let $\sigma$ be a permutation of $\{0,\ldots,n-1\}$. The
monomial associated with $\sigma$ has exponent $1$ on each variable indexed by
$(i,\sigma(i))$ and exponent $0$ on every other variable.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[Entries of a matching monomial]
\lean{Randomized.Matching.matchMono_apply}
\label{Randomized.Matching.matchMono_apply}
\leanok
\uses{Randomized.Matching.matchMono}
\difficulty{3}
Let $n$ be a natural number and let $\sigma$ be a permutation of the set
$\{0,\ldots,n-1\}$. Define a monomial by summing, over all indices $i$, the exponent
vector that assigns exponent $1$ to the variable indexed by $(i,\sigma(i))$ and $0$ to
all other variables. At a variable indexed by $(a,b)$, its exponent is $1$ if
$\sigma(a)=b$ and $0$ otherwise.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Injectivity of matching monomials]
\lean{Randomized.Matching.matchMono_injective}
\label{Randomized.Matching.matchMono_injective}
\leanok
\uses{Randomized.Matching.matchMono, Randomized.Matching.matchMono_apply}
\difficulty{4}
For every natural number $n$, the assignment sending a permutation of $\{0,\ldots,n-1\}$
to the monomial whose variables are precisely the pairs $(i,\sigma(i))$ is injective.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Product Along a Permutation]
\lean{Randomized.Matching.prod_edmondsMatrix}
\label{Randomized.Matching.prod_edmondsMatrix}
\leanok
\uses{Randomized.Matching.edmondsMatrix, Randomized.Matching.matchMono}
\difficulty{4}
Let $n$ be a natural number, let $R$ be a commutative semiring, let $A$ be a Boolean
matrix indexed by $\text{Fin}(n)\times\text{Fin}(n)$, and let $\sigma$ be a permutation
of $\text{Fin}(n)$. The product over $i\in\text{Fin}(n)$ of the entries of the Edmonds
matrix in positions $(i,\sigma(i))$ equals the monomial with coefficient $1$ and
exponent vector having exponent $1$ at each pair $(i,\sigma(i))$ if every such entry of
$A$ is true, and equals zero otherwise.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Determinant expansion by permutations]
\lean{Randomized.Matching.det_edmondsMatrix_eq_sum}
\label{Randomized.Matching.det_edmondsMatrix_eq_sum}
\leanok
\uses{Randomized.Matching.edmondsMatrix}
\difficulty{1}
Let $n$ be a nonnegative integer, let $R$ be a commutative ring, and let $A$ be an
$n\times n$ Boolean matrix. Form the polynomial matrix whose $(i,j)$ entry is $X_{i,j}$
when $A_{i,j}=\mathrm{true}$ and zero otherwise. Its determinant is the sum over all
permutations $\sigma$ of the indices of $\operatorname{sgn}(\sigma)$ times $\prod_i
M_{i,\sigma(i)}$, where $M$ is this polynomial matrix and the sign is viewed as a
polynomial over $R$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Determinant vanishes without a perfect matching]
\lean{Randomized.Matching.det_edmondsMatrix_eq_zero}
\label{Randomized.Matching.det_edmondsMatrix_eq_zero}
\leanok
\uses{Randomized.Matching.HasPerfectMatching, Randomized.Matching.det_edmondsMatrix_eq_sum, Randomized.Matching.edmondsMatrix, Randomized.Matching.hasPerfectMatching_iff_exists_perm}
\difficulty{4}
Let $n$ be a nonnegative integer, let $R$ be a commutative ring, and let $A$ be an
$n\times n$ Boolean matrix. If the bipartite graph with one copy of the indices on each
side and an edge from $i$ on the left to $j$ on the right exactly when
$A_{i,j}=\mathrm{true}$ has no perfect matching, then the determinant of the polynomial
matrix with entry $X_{i,j}$ at such edges and zero elsewhere is zero.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Matching monomial coefficient]
\lean{Randomized.Matching.coeff_det_edmondsMatrix}
\label{Randomized.Matching.coeff_det_edmondsMatrix}
\leanok
\uses{Randomized.Matching.det_edmondsMatrix_eq_sum, Randomized.Matching.edmondsMatrix, Randomized.Matching.matchMono, Randomized.Matching.matchMono_injective, Randomized.Matching.prod_edmondsMatrix}
\difficulty{5}
Let $n$ be a nonnegative integer, let $R$ be a commutative ring, and let $A$ be an
$n\times n$ matrix with entries in $\{\mathrm{false},\mathrm{true}\}$. For a permutation
$\tau$ of $\{0,\ldots,n-1\}$, suppose $A_{i,\tau(i)}=\mathrm{true}$ for every $i$. In
the determinant of the polynomial matrix whose $(i,j)$ entry is the indeterminate
$X_{i,j}$ when $A_{i,j}=\mathrm{true}$ and zero otherwise, the coefficient of $\prod_i
X_{i,\tau(i)}$ is the sign of $\tau$, viewed as an element of $R$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Determinant detects perfect matchings]
\lean{Randomized.Matching.det_edmondsMatrix_ne_zero_iff}
\label{Randomized.Matching.det_edmondsMatrix_ne_zero_iff}
\leanok
\uses{Randomized.Matching.HasPerfectMatching, Randomized.Matching.coeff_det_edmondsMatrix, Randomized.Matching.det_edmondsMatrix_eq_zero, Randomized.Matching.edmondsMatrix, Randomized.Matching.hasPerfectMatching_iff_exists_perm}
\difficulty{5}
Let $n$ be a nonnegative integer, let $R$ be a nontrivial commutative ring, and let $A$
be an $n\times n$ Boolean matrix. The determinant of the polynomial matrix with entry
$X_{i,j}$ when $A_{i,j}=\mathrm{true}$ and zero otherwise is nonzero if and only if the
associated bipartite graph, with an edge from left index $i$ to right index $j$ exactly
when $A_{i,j}=\mathrm{true}$, has a perfect matching.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Degree Bound for the Edmonds Determinant]
\lean{Randomized.Matching.totalDegree_det_edmondsMatrix_le}
\label{Randomized.Matching.totalDegree_det_edmondsMatrix_le}
\leanok
\uses{Randomized.Matching.det_edmondsMatrix_eq_sum, Randomized.Matching.edmondsMatrix}
\difficulty{4}
Let $n$ be a natural number, let $R$ be a commutative ring, and let $A$ be a Boolean
matrix indexed by $\text{Fin}(n)\times\text{Fin}(n)$. The total degree of the
determinant of the Edmonds matrix specified by $A$ is at most $n$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{definition}[Lovász matrix]
\lean{Randomized.Matching.lovaszMatrix}
\statementsource{arora-barak-ch07-randomized-computation}{pdf-26d95080dbde-p006-b001}
\label{Randomized.Matching.lovaszMatrix}
\leanok
Let $n$ be a natural number, let $R$ be a type with a zero element, let $A$ be an
$n\times n$ Boolean matrix, and let $a$ assign an element of $R$ to each pair of
indices. The associated matrix has entry $a(i,j)$ when $A_{ij}$ is true and $0$
otherwise.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[Evaluation of the Edmonds determinant]
\lean{Randomized.Matching.eval_det_edmondsMatrix}
\label{Randomized.Matching.eval_det_edmondsMatrix}
\leanok
\uses{Randomized.Matching.edmondsMatrix, Randomized.Matching.lovaszMatrix}
\difficulty{3}
Let $n$ be a natural number, let $R$ be a commutative ring, let $A$ be an $n\times n$
Boolean matrix, and let $a_{ij}\in R$ be specified for every pair of indices. Form the
polynomial matrix whose $(i,j)$ entry is the variable indexed by $(i,j)$ when $A_{ij}$
is true and zero otherwise, and evaluate its determinant by substituting $a_{ij}$ for
each variable. The result equals the determinant of the matrix with entries $a_{ij}$
where $A_{ij}$ is true and zero elsewhere.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Lovász determinant vanishes without a matching]
\lean{Randomized.Matching.det_lovaszMatrix_eq_zero}
\label{Randomized.Matching.det_lovaszMatrix_eq_zero}
\leanok
\uses{Randomized.Matching.HasPerfectMatching, Randomized.Matching.det_edmondsMatrix_eq_zero, Randomized.Matching.eval_det_edmondsMatrix, Randomized.Matching.lovaszMatrix}
\difficulty{1}
Let $n$ be a nonnegative integer, let $R$ be a commutative ring, and let $A$ be an
$n\times n$ Boolean matrix whose associated bipartite graph has no perfect matching. For
any weights $a_{i,j}\in R$, form the matrix with entry $a_{i,j}$ when
$A_{i,j}=\mathrm{true}$ and zero otherwise. Its determinant is zero.
\end{theorem}

\begin{definition}[Lovász sample function]
\lean{Randomized.Matching.lovaszSample}
\statementsource{arora-barak-ch07-randomized-computation}{pdf-26d95080dbde-p006-b001}
\label{Randomized.Matching.lovaszSample}
\leanok
\uses{Randomized.blockVal}
Let $R$ be a type with natural-number casts, and let $n$ and $k$ be natural numbers and
$l$ a Boolean list. The function on pairs of indices $(i,j)$ assigns the cast to $R$ of
the block value at the index corresponding to $(i,j)$ under the standard equivalence
between pairs of indices and indices in a product of two finite ranges.
\end{definition}

\difficulty{6}
Let $n,k$ be natural numbers, let $A$ be an $n\times n$ Boolean matrix whose bipartite
graph has a perfect matching, and let $R$ be a commutative domain. Assume $2n\le 2^k$
and the natural-number embedding into $R$ is injective on the integers from $0$ through
$2^k-1$. Choose a uniformly random bit string of length exactly $n^2k$, divide it into
consecutive blocks of $k$ bits, and interpret each block as a natural number. Form the
matrix that has these values, embedded in $R$, at the positions where $A$ is $1$, and
zero elsewhere. The probability that this matrix has nonzero determinant is at least
$1/2$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Truncating a Lovász sample]
\lean{Randomized.Matching.lovaszSample_take}
\label{Randomized.Matching.lovaszSample_take}

\difficulty{4}
Let $n,k$ be natural numbers, let $R$ be a type with a natural-number cast, and let $m$
be a natural number such that $n^2k\le m$. For every Boolean word $l$, the sample
constructed from the first $m$ bits of $l$ equals the sample constructed from all of
$l$.
\end{theorem}

\difficulty{3}
Let $n,k,m$ be natural numbers, let $A$ be an $n\times n$ Boolean matrix whose bipartite
graph has a perfect matching, and let $R$ be a commutative domain. Assume $2n\le 2^k$,
the natural-number embedding into $R$ is injective on the integers from $0$ through
$2^k-1$, and $n^2k\le m$. Choose a uniformly random bit string of length $m$; divide it
into consecutive blocks of $k$ bits and interpret each block as a natural number. Form
the matrix that has these values, embedded in $R$, at the positions where $A$ is $1$,
and zero elsewhere. The probability that this matrix has nonzero determinant is at least
$1/2$.
\end{theorem}

\difficulty{3}
Let $n,p,k,m$ be natural numbers, with $p$ prime, and let $A$ be an $n\times n$ Boolean
matrix whose bipartite graph has a perfect matching. Assume $2n\le 2^k\le p$ and
$n^2k\le m$. Choose a uniformly random bit string of length $m$, divide it into
consecutive blocks of $k$ bits, and interpret each block as a natural number modulo $p$.
Form the matrix over the field with $p$ elements that has these values at the positions
where $A$ is $1$, and zero elsewhere. The probability that this matrix has nonzero
determinant is at least $1/2$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Zero Acceptance Probability Without a Perfect Matching]
\lean{Randomized.Matching.randProb_lovasz_eq_zero}
\label{Randomized.Matching.randProb_lovasz_eq_zero}
\leanok
\uses{Randomized.Matching.HasPerfectMatching, Randomized.Matching.det_lovaszMatrix_eq_zero, Randomized.Matching.lovaszMatrix, Randomized.Matching.lovaszSample, Randomized.randProb, Randomized.randProb_congr, Randomized.randProb_false}
\difficulty{3}
Let $n,k,m$ be natural numbers, let $R$ be a commutative ring with decidable equality,
and let $A$ be a Boolean matrix indexed by $\text{Fin}(n)\times\text{Fin}(n)$. If the
bipartite graph specified by $A$ has no perfect matching, then the probability, for a
uniformly chosen $m$-bit string, that the determinant of the adjacency-masked matrix of
sampled entries over $R$ is nonzero is zero.
\end{theorem}
